Romans 16
ROH-muhnz six-TEEN
scripture portion
The closing chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans; a chapter of greetings to named saints and households.

📖 Biblical Definition

Romans 16 is the closing chapter of Paul’s great epistle, a long roll of greetings to named believers in the church at Rome, with a final warning and a soaring doxology. Far from a mere postscript, it is a precious window into the life of the early church. Paul commends Phebe, a servant of the church at Cenchrea, who bore the epistle; he greets Priscilla and Aquila, who had laid down their own necks for his life; he salutes whole households, kinsmen, fellow-prisoners, beloved laborers, and the church that met in a house. The chapter shows the warmth, particularity, and breadth of Christian fellowship—men and women, slave and free, Jew and Gentile, all one in Christ and named with affection. Paul adds a sharp warning to mark and avoid those who cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine learned, for such serve their own belly and by good words deceive the simple. The epistle closes with a doxology to the only wise God, who is able to establish the saints according to the gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ. The dictionary receives Romans 16 as a portrait of the household of faith: doctrine issues in love, the gospel gathers a named and varied people, and the same apostle who expounded sovereign grace knew and loved his brethren by name.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The closing chapter of Romans, a roll of affectionate greetings to named saints and households, with a warning against divisive teachers and a doxology to the only wise God.

expand to see more

ROMANS 16, the closing chapter of Paul’s epistle to the Romans.

A long roll of greetings to named believers and households in the church at Rome.

Commends Phebe, a servant of the church, and greets Priscilla and Aquila.

Warns the saints to mark and avoid those who cause divisions contrary to sound doctrine.

Closes with a doxology to the only wise God who establishes the saints.

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 16:1 — "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea:"

Rom 16:16 — "Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you."

Rom 16:17 — "Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them."

Rom 16:27 — "To God only wise, be glory through Jesus Christ for ever. Amen."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The chapter’s named greetings are mined to overturn the order of the church, reading honored fellow-laborers as proof of women in the ruling office.

expand to see more

The reigning corruption presses the named women of Romans 16—Phebe, Priscilla, Junia, and the rest—into an argument that Scripture sanctions women in the offices of teaching and ruling elder. The chapter honors these women warmly as servants, helpers, fellow-laborers, and hosts of the church, and the dictionary honors them too; the gospel dignifies and employs women in countless vital labors. But commendation as a fellow-worker is not appointment to the eldership, which Paul elsewhere reserves to qualified men, and the same apostle who greets these women wrote that he suffered not a woman to teach nor to usurp authority over the man.

The honest reading neither erases these women nor unmakes the order of the church. Phebe carried the epistle; Priscilla helped instruct Apollos; many women labored much in the Lord. The dictionary celebrates this without conscripting it for egalitarian revolt. The chapter’s real lesson is the breadth and warmth of the household of faith—a named and varied people, men and women together, gathered by sovereign grace and bound in love—and its closing warning to avoid those who divide the church contrary to the doctrine once learned.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The chapter’s greetings and commendations display the named fellowship of the early church and its bonds of love.

expand to see more

Greek aspazomai — to greet, salute; the verb that runs through the chapter’s roll of names.

Greek diakonos — servant, minister; Phebe a servant of the church at Cenchrea.

Greek sunergos — fellow-worker; Paul’s frequent title for his helpers.

The “holy kiss” — a customary greeting of affection among the early saints.

The closing doxology names the “only wise God” who establishes believers.

Usage

"Romans 16 is cited to show the warmth and breadth of early Christian fellowship."

"Its warning against divisive teachers is applied to guarding the church’s unity in truth."

"The named women are honored as laborers while the eldership remains reserved to men."
